Predicts how the result changes when only the side to move changes

steps.text: In **Distant opposition: the same fight from afar** you kept the opposition from a distance. Now the choice: **close** (one square between the kings) or **distant** (three or five squares between)? **Lateral** means the kings stand on one rank, sideways. A pawn on that line occupies a square, so the close form can be out of reach. Count first, then ask who is to move.

steps.caption: Kings on the sixth rank with five squares between them; one of those squares holds Black's pawn. White to move wins (tablebase).

steps.text: **When it matters.** The kings face each other on one line and the pawns are locked, so the side to move may have to give way. **When it fails.** In some positions the side to move does not decide the result at all. Do not assume the count alone decides it: in the first board the side to move wins. Count the squares, then test both sides to move.

steps.title: Kings on the second rank: who profits from the move?

steps.prompt: In the last positions, what did you check first: the squares between the kings, or the side to move? Where did your order of checks fail?

steps.text: **Remember.** When kings face each other on a line, count the squares between them, then check who is to move. Close opposition has one square between, distant has three or five. A pawn on the line can put the close form out of reach. It fails when the side to move does not decide the result, so test both sides to move.
